title: Depth of field — Image Wiki
text:
Depth of field
  The band of distance that comes out looking sharp. Everything outside it blurs, and how that blur grows tells you whether a picture came out of a real camera.

  
    Termdepth of field
    Also calledDoF, shallow focus, background blur, focus falloff
    Not the same asbokeh, motion blur, lens softness, focal length
    Read7 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat changes itWhat blur is forBokeh is not the amount of blurWhat to look for when judging an image
      
    
  

  The band of distance that comes out looking sharp is the depth of field. The useful part for judging pictures is not the definition but the shape of the falloff, because real optics blur in a very particular way and fakes usually do not.
First thing to unlearn: there is no line. Everything even slightly in front of or behind the focused distance is already losing sharpness — you just cannot see it yet.
Why it happens
A lens focuses exactly one distance. Light leaving a point at that distance passes through the whole opening and reconverges to a point on the sensor. That is what "in focus" means.

lenssensor240 units awaylands as a pointthe sensor’s-eye view, same scale in both panelsPoint at the focused distancethe cone converges exactly at the sensorlenssensor120 units awaylands as a discthe sensor’s-eye view, same scale in both panelsThe same point, moved to half that distancenothing else changed — not the lens, not the aperture, not the sensor

Same lens, same aperture, same sensor. The only thing that moves is the point in the scene.
Left: at the focused distance the cone reconverges exactly where the sensor is, so the point records as a point. Right: move the point nearer and its sharp image forms behind the sensor — the small circle past the sensor bar — so the sensor cuts a still-converging cone and gets a filled disc. A point beyond the focused distance images in front of the sensor and gets caught spreading again, same result. Move it further either way and the disc keeps growing.


That disc is the circle of confusion, and the threshold is perceptual, not optical: the image looks sharp until the discs get big enough for you to notice. Camera makers pick a disc about 0.01 inches across on a standard 8x10 inch print viewed from a foot away, which is where the depth-of-field marks on old lenses come from; Cambridge in Colour notes that 20/20 vision resolves a third of that.
So depth of field depends on how you look at the picture. Zoom to 100% and the discs grow with the image, so the sharp band shrinks. A shot that is fine as a thumbnail can be out of focus at full size.
What changes it

Aperture. A wide opening makes a steep cone, so the disc grows fast either side of focus and the band is thin; a small one makes a narrow cone and a thick band. Same control that sets exposure — see Exposure and dynamic range.
Focus distance. The biggest lever and the one people forget. Focus close and depth of field collapses: macro at high magnification has millimetres of depth at any aperture, so a beetle's eye can be sharp while its own antenna is gone. Focus far and the band stretches until, past the hyperfocal distance, everything to infinity is inside it.
Focal length. Handle with care; the internet gets this wrong in both directions. From a fixed position a longer lens gives visibly less depth of field, and that is the everyday case. But keep the subject the same size in the frame — closer with a wide lens, farther with a long one — and total depth of field barely moves: Cambridge in Colour's figures at f/4 are 0.482 m of depth for 10 mm at 0.5 m against 0.404 m for 200 mm at 10 m. Sources look like they disagree here only because they are answering different questions; both statements hold. The trap underneath is the one in Focal length vs camera position: changing lens usually means changing where you stand.
Sensor size. A bigger sensor needs a longer lens for the same framing, so less depth of field at the same f-number. Phones are sharp front to back and have to fake the blur; medium format looks the way it does for the opposite reason.



f/1.4
f/4
f/22


Alex1ruff, 2014. Five stacks of letter blocks receding from the camera, focus held on the front stack; only the aperture changed. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
At f/1.4 the front stack is crisp, the second is already soft and the fifth has dissolved into coloured shapes. At f/4 three stacks are readable. At f/22 all five are, down to the small "3" on the back block.
Watch the rate, not just the extent: at f/1.4 each stack is markedly softer than the one in front of it, a steep and continuous falloff along the receding line. That is what real optics does, and what blur painted on afterwards usually gets wrong.


Stopping all the way down does not keep helping. Past roughly f/11 to f/16 on most cameras, diffraction spreads every point into a disc of its own and the whole picture softens, focal plane included.
What blur is for
Blur is separation. A sharp subject on a soft field is the cheapest way of saying look here — see Visual hierarchy. It works by deletion, removing the competing detail that would otherwise pull the eye. The practical version is to step back and shoot long, so a cluttered background becomes one patch of colour.
Deep focus is a choice with its own job: landscape, architecture, group shots, anything where the relationship between near and far is the subject. Citizen Kane is the standing example, sharp from the foreground glass to the door at the back of the room, so the viewer has to choose where to look.
Bokeh is not the amount of blur
Bokeh is the character of the out-of-focus rendering, especially of small bright highlights. Depth of field only says where sharpness ends; two images with identical depth of field can have very different bokeh.
The shape comes from the diaphragm. Most lenses have 5 to 8 blades, so a defocused highlight only approximates a circle when it is small or the lens is wide open. Near the frame corners the discs often get clipped into cat's-eye shapes.



Kjoonlee, 2026, Heptagonal bokeh. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
Find the pale gaps of sky in the upper right, just past the leaves. They are not soft round blobs: each has straight sides and sharp corners, and the clearest are unambiguously seven-sided — the outline of the diaphragm, stamped on the image once per out-of-focus highlight. Below them, just right of the trunk, a lone turquoise highlight comes out as the same seven-sided shape in a different colour: the giveaway that the shape belongs to the lens, not to anything in the scene. Meanwhile the trunk and the nearest leaf edges are sharp enough to count veins.
Calling bokeh good or bad is taste; calling it heptagonal is fact.


What to look for when judging an image
Real optical blur is not a filter. It is geometry, so it obeys the scene:

Blur grows smoothly with distance from the focal plane. A background evenly blurred from the subject's shoulder to the horizon has no depth in it.
Equal distance means equal sharpness. An object sharp on one side and soft on the other at the same distance is wrong, and so is a sharp face with a soft hand beside it.
The boundary follows the object, not its outline. A thin sharp halo of background clinging to a silhouette, or a soft fringe eating into the subject, is a cutout.
Highlights should form discs that grow with distance. A smear where bright points stay points is blur applied afterwards. Hard light is what puts specular points in a scene at all (Hard and soft light), so a hard-lit background with no discs is doubly suspect.
Hair, whiskers and thin wires are where fakes break. Strands crossing the blur boundary should blur where they leave the focal plane.

One caveat before you flag anything. A sharp wedge running diagonally through a scene, instead of a plane parallel to the sensor, is what a tilt lens does: tilting the lens swings the plane of sharpest focus off perpendicular. The same trick in reverse makes the fake-miniature look. Odd focus geometry is a reason to look harder, not a verdict.

Five seconds on any blurred image

Find the sharpest point. Is everything at that distance equally sharp?
Follow a receding surface, a floor or a wall. Does it soften gradually, or in one step?
Look at a bright point light in the background. A disc with an edge, or a smudge?
Trace the subject's outline, especially hair and fingers. Any halo, any change in blur landing exactly on the silhouette?
Zoom in. Depth of field shrinks as you enlarge, so 1-4 get easier, not harder.
